title: Football Clubs With the Strangest Badges | WinFulltime
description: From Bournemouth's diving man to a cannon firing a ball. The strangest football club badges in the world and the stories behind them.
keywords: strangest football badges, weird club crests, Bournemouth badge diving header, Canon Yaounde badge, football crests history, strange football logos
h1: Football Clubs With the Strangest Badges
lead: Most club crests feature lions, castles or footballs. A few feature something far stranger — a diving man, a cannon firing a ball, or a telephone.
thumbCaption: The strangest football club badges in the world
share: A diving header, a cannon firing a football, a telephone — the strangest club badges in world football.
content:
A club badge is meant to say something about a club: its city, its history, its identity. Sometimes the message is a little garbled. Across world football, there are crests that raise questions every time they appear on a shirt — and a handful of them have become famous precisely because they are so strange.

The Man Who Never Stopped Diving: Bournemouth

The most famous 'strange badge' debate in England concerns AFC Bournemouth. Their crest appears to feature a man frozen in an odd crouching pose — and the explanation is genuinely lovely. The figure is Dickie Dowsett, a Bournemouth player from the late 1950s and early 60s, and the pose is his signature diving header. What looks like a strange silhouette is actually the club's most famous goalscorer, captured mid-flight. When the modern badge simplified the drawing, the man leaning forward became even harder to read — and the internet never let it go.

The Cannon That Fires a Ball: Canon Yaoundé

Cameroon's Canon Yaoundé was the dominant club of the 1970s and 80s, and their badge is unashamedly literal. It features a cannon — the club's name means 'cannon' in French — and the cannon is firing a football. It is one of the most distinctive crests in African football, and one of the few that shows the sport itself being launched from a weapon.

The Telephone Exchange: TOT SC

Thailand's TOT SC wear a badge that belongs in an office, not on a football pitch. TOT stood for the Telephone Organisation of Thailand, and the club's crest is a classic old-style rotary telephone — a piece of equipment most of the squad had probably never seen when the club was founded. The telephone badge became a cult favourite with crest collectors around the world.

The Missile: Missile FC

Gabon's Missile FC takes the 'named after something fast' tradition literally. The club's badge is a missile — a rocket mid-launch, with the club name across the bottom. It may not be subtle, but it is certainly unambiguous, and it makes the club one of the most recognisable crests in central Africa.

Industry on a Badge: Sheffield United

Some of football's strangest-looking badges are actually perfectly logical once you know the city. Sheffield United's crest shows two crossed items that look like oversized knives and forks. They are, in fact, blades — Sheffield is the steel city, home of cutlery and bladesmithing. The nickname 'the Blades' and the badge both celebrate the industry that built the city, even if the drawing reads more like a dinner setting to the uninitiated.

Why So Many Badges Look Odd

There is a pattern behind the world's strangest crests. Most were designed in an era before professional branding, when a club simply put its trade, its name or a local symbol on a shield and moved on:

  • Industrial clubs — hammers, blades, iron, miners' lamps and cannons appear wherever industry defined the town.
  • Name-based clubs — the crest often shows exactly what the name says (cannon, missile, telephone).
  • Honour-based clubs — the classic lions, crowns and castles that dominate European crests.
The takeaway: A strange badge is usually a badge that tells the truth. Bournemouth's diving man, Sheffield's blades and Canon's firing cannon all make perfect sense when you know the club — which is more than can be said for many boring, generic modern crests.

keywords: most unusual football kits, weird football shirts, Colchester LEGO kit, grey Manchester United shirt, unusual football kit designs, football shirt history
h1: The Most Unusual Football Kits Ever Worn
lead: Football kits are supposed to be simple: a shirt, some shorts, a club colour. Occasionally a club hands its players something far stranger — and the results go down in history.
thumbCaption: The most unusual football kits ever worn
share: A LEGO-brick shirt, a grey kit blamed for a defeat, camouflage stripes — the most unusual football kits ever worn.
content:
For most of football's history, a kit meant a plain shirt in the club colour, worn with pride. Then someone realised that a shirt could be a billboard, a fashion statement and occasionally a public experiment. The result is a collection of kits so unusual that they are remembered decades later.

The Grey Shirt That Caused a Defeat: Manchester United

The most notorious kit in English football history is Manchester United's grey away shirt of 1995-96. In April 1996, United wore it against Southampton and lost 3-1 — a result manager Alex Ferguson blamed squarely on the kit. His players could not pick each other out against the crowd's white shirts, he claimed, and United changed into their blue-and-white away strip at half-time. The grey kit was quietly retired, but it never stopped being famous. Ferguson even had a rule written into United's contracts: no grey away kit.

The LEGO Kit: Colchester United

In 2016-17, League One side Colchester United released a third kit that looked exactly like a red LEGO brick — complete with a row of studs across the chest. The design was a clever nod to the town's famous LEGO manufacturing heritage and the company's founder, Ole Kirk Christiansen, who ran a joiner's workshop in the area. It was a marketing phenomenon: the shirt sold out worldwide, turned Colchester into an internet sensation, and remains the most famous non-league-of-fame kit of the modern era.

Camouflage Football: Udinese

In 2018-19, Serie A's Udinese unveiled a third shirt in full camouflage print — a military-style pattern that made the players blend into the stadium rather than stand out. The kit was a tribute to the club's nickname, 'Zebrette' (little zebras), with the camouflage rendered in the club's black and white. It was one of the most polarising shirts of the season, loved by collectors and mocked by traditionalists.

Sporting CP's Tribute Kits

Sporting Clube de Portugal have built a habit of unusual tribute shirts. Their 2024-25 third kit was designed as a tribute to the club's greatest product, Cristiano Ronaldo, with details drawn from his career — a rare case of a club kit designed around a player's story rather than the club's colours.

Why Kits Get Weird

Unusual kits rarely happen by accident. There are usually three forces at work:

  • Marketing — a distinctive third kit sells shirts worldwide, especially to collectors.
  • Heritage — clubs celebrate local industries (Colchester's LEGO) or nicknames (Udinese's zebras).
  • Manufacturer creativity — kit makers compete to produce the most talked-about design of the season.
The rule of thumb: A genuinely unusual kit is a bet — either it becomes a classic, or it becomes a cautionary tale. The grey United shirt became both.

title: Why Football Clubs Play in Unusual Colours | WinFulltime
description: Arsenal wear red because of Nottingham Forest, Juventus wear black and white from Notts County. Why clubs play in their unusual colours.
keywords: why clubs play in unusual colours, Arsenal red origin, Juventus black white Notts County, Barcelona colours Basel, Athletic Bilbao Southampton, football kit colour origins
h1: Why Some Football Clubs Play in Unusual Colours
lead: Why do Arsenal play in red? Why do Juventus wear black and white stripes? Most club colours were not chosen — they were borrowed, gifted or inherited.
thumbCaption: Why some football clubs play in unusual colours
share: Arsenal's red came from Nottingham Forest and Juventus's stripes from Notts County. The bizarre origins of football club colours.
content:
Ask most fans why their club wears its colours and the answer is usually 'tradition'. But tradition has to start somewhere — and for a surprising number of the world's biggest clubs, that starting point was a gift, a chance meeting or a coincidence that happened over a century ago.

Arsenal Red: A Gift From Nottingham Forest

Arsenal play in red with white sleeves, and they have the famous gift to thank. In 1886, when the club was founded in south-east London as Dial Square, the founders were two former Nottingham Forest players. They had no kit, so Forest — one of the biggest clubs of the era — donated a set of their own red shirts. Arsenal have worn red ever since, and the white sleeves were added later as a design flourish.

Juventus Black and White: Straight From Notts County

Italy's most successful club wears stripes that were literally borrowed from an English club. In 1903, Juventus asked their English-born players to source a kit that would be more striking than their original pink shirts. The players asked their contacts in England, and Notts County — one of the oldest clubs in the world — sent over a set of black-and-white striped shirts. Juventus liked them so much they never changed, and the 'bianconeri' were born.

Athletic Bilbao: The Southampton Connection

Spain's Athletic Bilbao wear red and white stripes, and the origin story involves Southampton. In 1910, a Basque player named Juanito Elorduy returned from England with red-and-white shirts he had bought in Southampton — either from the Saints themselves or on their model. Bilbao adopted them the same year, and the colours spread to become the defining kit of Basque football.

Barcelona: The Basel Story

Barcelona's famous blaugrana — blue and garnet stripes — are the subject of several origin stories. The most popular version links the colours to FC Basel in Switzerland, through the club's founder, Swiss-born Hans Gamper, and a friend who provided shirts in the colours of the Swiss club. The story is repeated in club histories, though the exact details are debated. What is certain is that Barcelona have worn blue and garnet since the very beginning of the club in 1899.

AC Milan: 'Red Like Fire, Black to Invoke Fear'

AC Milan's red and black stripes were chosen by Herbert Kilpin, the English founder of the club, who explained the meaning directly: red for the fire of the club's spirit, and black to invoke fear in opponents. That explanation, passed down in club legend, is one of the few colour origins with a stated philosophy behind it.

Liverpool All Red: Shankly's Decision

Liverpool are now inseparable from all-red, but the club wore white shorts and red shirts for most of its history. The all-red kit arrived in 1964, when manager Bill Shankly decided the psychological impact of an entirely red outfit would intimidate opponents. Liverpool wore the new kit at Anderlecht and won 3-0; the colour scheme has been the club's identity ever since.

Celtic's Hoops and West Ham's Claret

Celtic adopted their green-and-white hoops in 1903, in a deliberate nod to their Irish identity and the green of Ireland. West Ham United, meanwhile, have worn claret and sky blue since the club's earliest days in the early 1900s, with the famous claret shirt with sky-blue sleeves established by 1904 — a look that has barely changed in more than a century.

ClubColoursOrigin
ArsenalRedDonated by Nottingham Forest, 1886

Athletic BilbaoRed & white stripesFrom Southampton, 1910

The pattern: The most unusual club colours in football were almost never chosen from a catalogue. They were inherited — from a donated kit, a cross-Channel shopping trip or a manager's hunch about psychology.

title: The Most Famous Football Mascots in the World | WinFulltime
description: Gunnersaurus, Fred the Red, Moonchester and Naranjito. The most famous football mascots in the world, from clubs to World Cups.
keywords: famous football mascots, Gunnersaurus, Fred the Red, Moonchester, World Cup mascots, Naranjito Fuleco, football club mascots
h1: The Most Famous Football Mascots in the World
lead: Behind every great club is a giant foam dinosaur, a swan in a wedding dress or an orange with a football face. These are the most famous mascots in football.
thumbCaption: The most famous football mascots in the world
share: Gunnersaurus, Fred the Red, Naranjito — the most famous football mascots from clubs and World Cups.
content:
Mascots exist to entertain children, lighten the mood and — in the modern era — sell merchandise. But the very best ones transcend that job description entirely, becoming symbols that fans grow up with and defend with genuine passion.

Gunnersaurus: The Dinosaur That Refused to Die

The most famous mascot in world football is Gunnersaurus Rex, Arsenal's seven-foot-tall green dinosaur. He debuted in August 1994 against Manchester City, designed by an 11-year-old fan named Peter Lovell, and was worn by the same man, Jerry Quy, for more than 25 years. When Arsenal announced in October 2020 that Gunnersaurus would be made redundant during the pandemic, the football world reacted with fury — Mesut Özil even offered to pay his salary himself. The club reversed the decision within weeks, and Gunnersaurus remains one of the most loved figures in English football.

Cyril the Swan: The Mascot Who Got Married

Cyril the Swan of Swansea City has been entertaining crowds since 1998, and his fame comes with a genuinely unique story: in 2005, Cyril 'married' another mascot, Cybil, in a ceremony that made headlines across Britain. He is one of the few mascots in the world with his own wedding, and remains the heart of Swansea's matchday entertainment.

The Big English Club Mascots

Every major English club now has its own character, and several have become stars in their own right:

MascotClubFun fact
Fred the RedManchester UnitedOne of the longest-serving mascots in English football
MoonchesterManchester CityAn alien — reportedly from the Moon
Stamford the LionChelseaThe Stamford Bridge lion
Harry the HornetWatfordAdopted in 2000
HammerheadWest Ham UnitedNamed for the club's hammer identity
Mighty RedLiverpoolIntroduced in 2012

The World Cup Mascots

The most famous football mascots of all are the World Cup's official characters, because each one represents a host nation to a global audience:

  • Naranjito — the orange in a Spanish kit, mascot of the 1982 World Cup in Spain, and one of the most iconic mascots in sporting history.
  • Fuleco — the three-banded armadillo, mascot of the 2014 World Cup in Brazil, named from 'futebol' and 'ecologia'.
  • La'eeb — the keffiyeh-clad character of the 2022 World Cup in Qatar, described as a 'super-skilled player'.

Earlier editions produced legends too: World Cup Willie in 1966 was the first World Cup mascot ever, and the Spanish orange Naranjito remains the standard against which every tournament mascot is judged.

Why Mascots Matter

It is easy to mock mascots, but they perform a serious function. They are the connection point between a club and its youngest fans — the first character a child meets on the way to the turnstiles. When Gunnersaurus was almost scrapped, the backlash showed exactly how deep that bond runs.

The unsung stars: The people inside the suits do the real work. Jerry Quy wore the Gunnersaurus costume for 25 years, through rain, snow and heat — the longest-serving mascot performer in the English game.

title: The Most Bizarre Football Match Delays Ever | WinFulltime
description: Floodlight failures, streakers and a referee who sent off the wrong player. The most bizarre football match delays in history.
keywords: bizarre football match delays, floodlight failure match, abandoned matches, Mark Roberts streaker, referee mistaken identity, weird match delays
h1: The Most Bizarre Football Match Delays Ever
lead: Matches get delayed for weather and injuries. Occasionally they are delayed for something else entirely — a lights failure, a streaker, or a referee's catastrophic mix-up.
thumbCaption: The most bizarre football match delays ever
share: Lights going out, a streaker at the FA Cup final, and a referee who sent off the wrong player — football's most bizarre delays.
content:
A football match is supposed to start on time and finish ninety minutes later. In the vast majority of cases, it does. But football's entire history contains a glorious collection of exceptions — matches held up or abandoned for reasons no rulebook could have predicted.

The Floodlight Failures

Floodlight failure is football's most dramatic technical delay: an entire stadium plunges into darkness with a game in progress. Two of the most famous incidents happened in consecutive decades:

  • In August 1997, the Premier League match between Derby County and Wimbledon was abandoned after 56 minutes when the floodlights at the Baseball Ground failed. The game restarted later and was replayed.
  • In September 2004, a Scotland friendly against Spain in Valencia was abandoned on 59 minutes for exactly the same reason, with the entire stadium going dark mid-match.

Floodlight failures are surprisingly common across the lower leagues, where aging electrical systems struggle under load — and every one produces the same surreal image: players standing in darkness, waiting to be told what happens next.

The Streaker Problem

No delay in football is more bizarre than the streaker, and no streaker is more famous than Mark Roberts. By his own count he has run across pitches more than 580 times in over 20 countries, in every major competition — including the FA Cup final and a UEFA Cup final. His stunts have halted matches, emptied security details and produced some of the most photographed moments in sport. In one notorious incident at an England match he took the ball from a player mid-attack.

The Referee's Mistaken Identity

One of the strangest referee errors in World Cup history caused a different kind of delay: a red card shown to the wrong man. At the 2002 World Cup quarter-final between Germany and the United States, referee Hugh Dallas reached for his cards after a foul and sent off Germany's Oliver Neuville — but the offender was actually Jens Jeremies. Neuville left the pitch in disbelief, and the confusion took several minutes to sort out as the officials realised the error. The wrong man was eventually restored, but the incident remains one of the most famous officiating blunders in the tournament's history.

The Weather of a Different Kind

Beyond rain and snow, there have been delays caused by conditions that nobody plans for:

  • Dense fog has caused several matches to be abandoned or played in near-invisible conditions, most notoriously in England in the 1960s and 70s.
  • Birds on the pitch have halted play while players and officials shooed them off — a regular comedy routine at lower-league grounds.
  • Animals have made occasional appearances, from stray dogs to a reported snake on the pitch during a Brazilian match.

The Longest Delays

The longest delays in football history are not caused by any of the above but by the elements — specifically the English winter of 1963, when snow and ice forced the cancellation of entire football weekends. Those cancellations belong in our guide to extreme weather, because they did not just delay one match; they shut down a whole season.

The common thread: Whether it is a floodlight, a streaker or a referee's mistake, a bizarre delay reminds everyone — players, fans and broadcasters — that football is a human game, and humans are unpredictable.
